extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetry/literary criticism; poets interested in classical poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles drawn from Aristotelian and classical Greek theory for judging or composing poetry and drama, emphasising universality, coherence, restraint, and poetic truth. Useful for assessing how a work handles character, myth/history, imagination, and the plausible presentation of the irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy vs Tragedy — individual vs type/universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy tends to merge the individual into the type; tragedy combines in one harmonious representation the individual and the universal. 'Comedy...creates personified ideals, tragedy creates idealised persons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, note whether it treats characters as exemplars of a social/type role (comic typification) or uses particular individuals to manifest universal human possibilities (tragic idealisation). The effectiveness depends on coherence with the genre's aim: comedy generalises to type; tragedy particularises to reveal the universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pure realism (literal/prosaic imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure realism is forbidden; that is, the literal and prosaic imitation which reaches perfection in a jugglery of the senses by which the copy is mistaken for the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid evaluating a poem positively simply because of hyper-detailed sensory mimicry. Anti-pattern: art that aims to reproduce surface detail so exactly that it substitutes for imaginative truth (e.g., portrait-like memorial realism). Prefer imaginative representation that captures truth without slavish literalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pure symbolism (grotesque/implausible compounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure symbolism is forbidden—those fantastic shapes which attempt to render abstract attributes in forms which do not correspond with the idea (e.g., impossible animal-human hybrids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic invention must still correspond intelligibly to the idea it signifies. Avoid fanciful emblematic forms that violate nature's laws and therefore break the reader's sense of intelligibility and poetic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth / internal plausibility of the irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational or impossible elements (τὰ ἄλογα) are acceptable only as accessories that do not disturb the main impression; when presented with vividness and coherence the impossible becomes plausible (the fiction looks like truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether supernatural or fantastical elements are integrated coherently so they enhance rather than disrupt the overall believable impression. Success = the reader accepts the impossible because it is presented with internal consistency and vivid detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperate restraint, harmony, and avoidance of ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek imagination is under the strict control of reason, limited by a sense of measure and a faculty of self-restraint. The artist employs power without effort and without ostentation; he is bent on seeing truly, on seeing harmoniously, and on expressing what he sees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that show controlled power: expressive economy, clarity, and harmonious composition rather than dazzling virtuosity for its own sake. Anti-pattern: gratuitous excess that distracts from unity and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled inspiration: imagination must obey reason and hidden law
rubrics_metrics.description: Even those poets whose genius seems 'ecstatic' never released themselves from the sovereignty of reason; their most fantastic creations obey a hidden law and are not capricious or inconsequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge inspiration against criterion of control—original flights of imagination should still exhibit internal logic, consistency of character and motive, and contribute to the poem's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality: represent permanent possibilities, not mere accident
rubrics_metrics.description: The effort of poetry is towards the universal; it represents the permanent possibilities of human nature, the essentials rather than the accidents. The poet tells what may happen according to laws of internal probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether characters and events reveal larger human truths or laws of human behaviour rather than merely reporting contingent particulars. Strong poetry illuminates general human possibilities through particular instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical/conceivable sequence and elimination of chance
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequence of poetry is not the empirical sequence of fact but the logical or conceivable sequence of ideas; it eliminates chance and discovers unity and significance in characters and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plot and event ordering for internal necessity and meaningful causation. Random coincidences or improbabilities that undermine logical coherence are faults; events should follow from character and necessity or credible probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as types with depth (typification balanced with individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek heroines are broadly and unmistakably human and reducible to elemental types (maiden, wife, mother, daughter, sister). In discarding accidental detail their individuality is not obliterated but deepened: the finer shades of character are admitted if they contribute to the total impression and unity of design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good characterisation often trades excessive idiosyncrasy for typified clarity while preserving depth: judge whether the type illuminates universal aspects without flattening the character's internal complexity that matters to the work's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as concrete philosophy / 'criticism of life'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is a concrete philosophy, 'a criticism of life'—it employs sensuous and imaginative form to embody an interpretation of man, life, and the world; poems (especially the highest) contain a latent, consistent view essential to their unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a poem or play embodies a coherent, harmonious wisdom or interpretive stance about human life. Even if not systematised, the underlying philosophical shape should be perceptible and integral to the work's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myth and historical perspective to elevate the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth was the unwritten literature of an early people; poets connect the present with the mythic past so that the individual (e.g., a victor) is transfigured into a personification of his race; poetry projects the present into the past to achieve larger meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how effectively a work situates its particulars within larger historical/mythic frames to gain universality and distance from immediate pain or parochiality. Anti-pattern: using recent, raw events without the detachment needed for poetic elevation (cf. fineing of Phrynichus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain fantasy so it does not disturb serenity of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside comedy, fancy is much more restrained in Greek literature; it breaks through as sudden and transient gleams and does not disturb the serenity of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value carefully modulated use of fancy—occasional imaginative flashes that deepen the work are good; sustained, uncontrolled extravagance that disrupts coherence is a defect.
